themes.name: Memory Supply Chain
themes.whatChanged: The shortage escalated sharply past what was already described as structural. Samsung and SK Hynix's finished DRAM inventory fell below 10 days of supply on September 7 — the tightest point of the cycle. SK Hynix says its HBM, DRAM, and NAND capacity is essentially sold out for all of 2026. Micron has exited the consumer memory market entirely to focus only on enterprise and AI customers. DRAM spot prices are up roughly 700% over the past year, far beyond the price rise already priced into this theme. Samsung's memory chief now expects significant shortages to continue through at least 2027, and SK Hynix isn't targeting new cleanroom capacity until 2028-2029.

portfolioImpact.reason: The thesis didn’t just play out, it accelerated — a 700% spot price move and sold-out 2026 capacity is pricing power with no near-term ceiling.
HBM demand is the direct cause of the shortage; NVDA sits upstream of it as the demand driver, and sold-out 2026 capacity confirms it isn’t slowing.
Buys mobile DRAM at enormous scale. A ~700% input cost move (up from the 80% figure this theme opened with) is a materially larger gross-margin threat than first described.
Server memory costs rise, but Azure pricing absorbs it and AI revenue growth outweighs the input hit — unchanged, though worth re-checking if the escalation continues.

themes.watch: Whether new cleanroom capacity (SK Hynix isn't targeting any until 2028-2029) starts before demand does, whether Micron's full exit from consumer memory pushes AAPL toward alternative suppliers, and whether spot prices keep climbing past +700%.

themes.name: Fed & Rates
themes.whatChanged: The PPI-CPI gap has barely narrowed heading into the September 17 FOMC decision — PPI at 9.85% year over year against CPI at 3.71%, still roughly a 6-point gap. What's new: the Hormuz-driven oil shock (see Defense & Geopolitics) adds a fresh inflation input right at the moment the Fed has to decide whether to cut, and the 10-year Treasury has already climbed to 4.96% from 4.63% in early August — the market pricing in some of that risk ahead of the decision.

themes.name: AI Infrastructure
themes.whatChanged: The capex story didn't just hold, it grew. The big four hyperscalers (Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, Google) now guide to roughly $732.5 billion in combined 2026 capex — up about 77% year over year — with H1 2026 actual spend alone already at $301 billion. Demand for AI infrastructure capacity is outpacing even this: hyperscale operators say they can't build data centers fast enough to keep up.

portfolioImpact.reason: Direct beneficiary. Hyperscaler capex converts almost mechanically into NVDA revenue, and guidance just got raised, not cut.
Both a spender and a seller — Azure AI revenue is the return on that capex.
Heavily weighted to exactly these names, which cuts both ways but is working now.

themes.watch: Whether actual spend through Q3/Q4 tracks the raised guidance, or any hyperscaler signals a pullback — the single point of failure for this theme hasn't changed, the stakes just got bigger.

themes.name: Tariffs
themes.whatChanged: Talks moved past the procedural stage. As of September 10, negotiators are actively working reciprocal cuts of roughly $30 billion in tariffs on each side's 'nonsensitive' goods, as part of broader talks toward a bilateral Board of Trade. A truce expires November 10, creating real urgency, and a leaders' meeting was expected within about two weeks of that date. Targeted reductions look more likely than a comprehensive deal.

portfolioImpact.reason: Largest China manufacturing exposure you own. Genuine upside if the Nov 10 deadline produces a deal, genuine risk if talks stall and the truce lapses — still unresolved in both directions.
China export restrictions matter more to NVDA than tariffs per se; this negotiation doesn’t address them.
Active tariff-reduction talks are broadly supportive of Chinese and Asian equities, which anchor most EM indices, more so now than at the procedural stage.

themes.watch: Whether the leaders' meeting (expected within about two weeks of Sep 10) produces an actual signed schedule before the November 10 truce deadline, or whether talks stall and the truce lapses.

themes.name: Defense & Geopolitics
themes.whatChanged: The Hormuz de-escalation from early August reversed. Strikes between the US and Iran intensified again in early September, and vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has effectively collapsed — from 100+ ships a day to roughly 5-12. The IEA has called it the largest oil supply disruption in the history of the global oil market, on the order of 20 million barrels a day removed. WTI has moved from the high-$80s to $97+/bbl in under two weeks; Brent is trading near $104-105. Forecasts diverge sharply on what happens next: Goldman Sachs’ base case has Brent easing back toward $85, while Rystad Energy’s scenario puts it above $140 with global recession risk attached.

portfolioImpact.reason: Oil feeds directly into CPI/PPI — the same PPI-CPI gap already flagged in the Fed & Rates theme — and a fresh inflation input makes a near-term rate cut less likely. Cash keeps earning while that persists.
Exposed on two fronts: an oil-driven inflation resurgence delays the cut equities are priced for, and the Rystad scenario attaches outright recession risk if the Strait stays effectively closed.
The most liquidity-sensitive holding here — a risk-off shock this size, on top of an already-elevated-rate environment, is a direct headwind, not the mixed read a de-escalation would have been.

themes.watch: Whether the Strait reopens to normal traffic or the closure persists — Goldman’s $85 base case and Rystad’s $140+/recession scenario diverge entirely on that question. The Sep 17 FOMC decision (already tracked below) is now also a referendum on whether the Fed treats this inflation input as transitory or persistent.

themes.name: Emerging Markets
themes.whatChanged: China's picture got more nuanced, not clearer: the official NBS manufacturing PMI improved slightly to 49.8 in August (from 49.2) but stayed in contraction for a second straight month, while the private Caixin PMI showed outright expansion at 51.5 — official and private surveys are telling different stories. India's RBI held its repo rate at 5.25% for a fourth consecutive meeting, citing a weakening rupee and Middle East-driven uncertainty. Brazil paused its cutting cycle at 14.25% after three straight cuts, and raised its own 2026 inflation projection to 5.2% — above its 4.5% ceiling.

themes.watch: Whether China's official and private PMI readings converge in September, and whether Brazil's paused cutting cycle resumes or holds given the higher inflation projection.

themes.name: Crypto / Bitcoin
themes.whatChanged: Bitcoin's price and its regulatory backdrop both moved this week. The Senate failed to advance the CLARITY Act (crypto market-structure legislation) in a 49-50 cloture vote on September 15 — short of the 60 needed — effectively killing it for 2026 and, given midterm politics, likely until 2029. Unresolved fights over DeFi treatment, stablecoin yield, and an ethics clause barring officials from launching tokens were the sticking points. The SEC's fallback path continues regardless: a formal 'Regulation Crypto Assets' rulemaking proposed August 19, with a 60-day comment period closing in mid-October. Separately, price has slid to around $77,000 ahead of the September 17 FOMC decision, down from an early-September peak near $81,000 after a short squeeze that had carried it up from below $63,000 — directly reflecting the same 'higher-for-longer' pressure already tracked in Fed & Rates. Spot Bitcoin ETF adoption keeps deepening in absolute terms regardless: $83.3 billion in net assets on $53.9 billion of cumulative inflows, even though 2026 flows overall remain net negative by more than $1 billion.

Near-term price is also under the same Fed-timing pressure already tracked in Fed & Rates.

themes.watch: Whether the SEC's Regulation Crypto Assets comment period (closing mid-October) produces an actual rule now that legislative action is off the table until at least 2029, and whether the Sep 17 FOMC decision reverses or extends the current price slide.
